USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Take a deal to the G20 in Argentina while keeping the scheduled January 1 escalation of the $200B List 3 tariffs from 10% to 25% firmly in reserve as leverage. Do not concede anything new — China has made no substantive offers and talks remain on hold (Kudlow: “we’re not on the cusp of a deal”) — but open a genuine negotiating channel given the Trump-Xi phone call on November 1 and the market’s hunger for a truce. Use the G20 as the forum to exchange concrete terms, not a place to escalate or to capitulate.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate, not severe. The US is the party imposing and escalating tariffs ($50B + $200B in place, ~$250B covered, with $267B threatened), so it holds the initiative and leverage rather than absorbing damage. Domestic macro remains firm — industrial production ~104 and rising, consumer sentiment ~97.5, and the dollar index climbing ~4.4% — so there is no material GDP drag or existential risk yet (country_health). What justifies a +0.2 rather than neutral is real, tangible cost: China’s retaliation is hitting the farm belt (soybeans) and created domestic political pressure that Trump himself acknowledged by turning conciliatory right before the midterms (Reuters/NYT); corporate credit stress is creeping (Baa yield up from 4.81 to 5.18 over the window); and the October equity selloff shows markets are fragile to further escalation. On the action side, negotiate at 0.0 is the right stance: escalating further now would spook fragile markets, raise consumer prices right after an election, and squander a rare presidential-level off-ramp, while conceding without Chinese commitments would forfeit hard-won leverage with nothing secured. Holding the 25% threat as a credible lever while engaging in talks maximizes the chance of extracting the structural commitments US leverage was built to obtain.
key_factors: US holds the escalation/leverage position (~$250B of tariffs in place, $267B threatened)
Nov 1 Trump-Xi phone call and scheduled G20 meeting open a negotiated off-ramp
US macro firm (industrial production rising, sentiment ~97.5, dollar up ~4.4%)
China's soybean retaliation hurts the farm belt and drove Trump's pre-midterm conciliatory tone
Corporate credit stress rising (Baa 4.81 to 5.18) and October equity selloff signal market fragility to further escalation
Jan 1 List 3 escalation to 25% is the natural lever to hold while negotiating

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold our current retaliatory posture but signal readiness to negotiate at the G20 meeting agreed in the Nov 1 Trump-Xi call, with the concrete goal of freezing the threatened Jan 1 escalation of List 3 from 10% to 25%. Offer incremental US import purchases as a face-saving path to a truce, but make no structural concessions on IP/tech-transfer before talks bear fruit. Do not escalate further, as escalation risks drawing US coverage of all Chinese exports onto a broader battlefield at a moment our currency and reserves are already under pressure.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential. By decision date the US had already locked in ~$250B of tariffs on Chinese goods (List 1+2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% since Sept 24) with List 3 scheduled to jump to 25% on Jan 1, and Trump has threatened to extend tariffs to effectively all Chinese exports (~$500B+). That is a direct, material hit to the export economy. Simultaneously the yuan has lost ~9-10% versus the dollar and is pressing toward the 7.0 level, FX reserves fell a record ~$34B in October to an 18-month low of ~$3.05T, and the PBOC was forced to act (hiking the short-yuan reserve requirement to 20% and cutting bank reserve ratios to support a slowing economy). Offsetting these, China's exports remained surprisingly resilient in the short run — September exports rose ~15% y/y — but that strength is sustained by order front-loading ahead of the January hike and is not durable; the economy is still growing near its ~6.5% target with ample reserves, and Beijing retains policy levers (retaliation, easing, trade diversification). This lands between the +0.5 'high' anchor and the existential threshold. On action: with a leaders' meeting at the G20 now agreed, the rational move is to negotiate rather than escalate — escalation would legitimize a US move to blanket coverage and the 25% rate at a time of FX and reserve strain. De-escalation to full concession is premature, since talks are not yet advanced and there is no matching US offer; 'negotiate' — maintain posture, seek a freeze on the Jan 1 hike via purchases — is the calibrated stance.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports tariffed (List 1+2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%), rising to 25% Jan 1 2019
Trump threat to extend tariffs to all ~$500B+ of Chinese exports
Yuan down ~9-10% vs USD, pressing toward 7.0
FX reserves fell a record ~$34B in Oct to 18-month low ~$3.05T
PBOC measures: raised short-yuan reserve req to 20%, cut bank reserve ratio (easing)
Exports resilient short-term via order front-loading, unsustainable
Nov 1 Trump-Xi call agreeing to G20 meeting = diplomatic opening
China economy still growing near ~6.5% target with ample reserves, giving policy levers
